The gonadosomatic index (GSI) of Beardfish (Polymixia lowei) has been reported at approximately 2% [GSI = approximately 2%] at a temperature of 13.4 °C [T = 13.4 °C]. This remarkably low reproductive investment relative to body mass is derived from comparative data on the closely related species Polymixia nobilis and suggests a strategy of protracted gamete production rather than a single, high-effort spawning pulse. The maintenance of such a low index likely reflects the energetic constraints of the mesopelagic environment, where food availability is sporadic and metabolic demands are narrowly balanced. Female Beardfish appear to allocate resources conservatively toward ovarian development, a pattern that aligns with the relatively modest ultimate body size observed in this species. Such a reproductive strategy is not uncommon among deep-dwelling teleosts that experience low and unpredictable prey densities, as the energetic risk of a high-investment spawning event would be substantial. Further histological examination of ovarian tissue could confirm whether this low index corresponds to continuous low-level vitellogenesis or a more punctuated cycle of oocyte recruitment.

The maximum recorded total length for Beardfish reaches 29.4 centimeters [Li = 29.4 centimeters], a size that defines the asymptotic upper boundary of somatic growth for this species. This ultimate length is modest when compared to many other members of the order Polymixiiformes, but it is consistent with a life-history strategy prioritizing longevity over rapid attainment of large body dimensions. Field surveys and trawl samples indicate that individuals approaching this length are relatively uncommon, suggesting that the population age structure is dominated by younger, smaller fish. The corresponding ultimate wet weight, calculated from a length-weight relationship, is 304.6 grams [Wwi = 304.6 grams], representing the maximum mass an adult Beardfish can be expected to achieve under natural conditions. This mass is attained gradually over many years, a trajectory that contrasts with the faster growth rates observed in epipelagic congeners that inhabit more productive surface waters. The allometric exponent used in the length-weight conversion implies slight positive allometry, meaning that larger individuals are somewhat heavier per unit length than their smaller counterparts. This pattern is typical of species that invest in robust axial musculature for sustained swimming in the deep-water column.

Onset of reproductive capability in Beardfish is signaled by the attainment of a fork length of 15 centimeters [Lp = 15 centimeters], marking the size threshold for puberty. The corresponding wet weight at this developmental stage is approximately 39.4 grams [Wwp = approximately 39.4 grams], a mass that represents a considerable fraction of the ultimate adult body mass. This early pubertal size suggests that individuals begin to allocate energy toward gonadal maturation well before they reach their full somatic potential, a pattern reminiscent of many slow-growing, deep-water teleosts that hedge their reproductive bets across a long lifespan. The fork length at puberty, measured from the snout to the fork of the caudal fin, is a standard ichthyological metric that facilitates comparisons with related species within the genus. Achieving this size typically requires several years of growth under the cold, food-limited conditions of the continental slope. The relatively low mass at puberty, compared to ultimate mass, indicates that Beardfish maintain a prolonged period of adult growth after the onset of reproductive maturity, allowing them to increase fecundity with age. This growth trajectory is consistent with an iteroparous life history wherein reproductive output scales with body size.

Eggs of Beardfish have a diameter of approximately 1 millimeter, which translates to a calculated wet weight at birth of 0.00052 grams [Wwb = 0.00052 grams] per individual larva upon hatching. This minute initial mass is typical of pelagic-spawning teleosts that produce numerous small offspring as a means of dispersing risk across a vast and unpredictable oceanic environment. At a water temperature of 13.4 °C [T = 13.4 °C], the yolk-sac larva, or alevin, relies entirely on its endogenous yolk reserves during the first few days after eclosion, undergoing rapid differentiation of the digestive tract and sensory organs. The chorion rupture and subsequent larval eclosion mark the transition to a free-swimming, planktonic existence during which the probability of mortality is exceedingly high. The tiny size of the newly hatched larva renders it vulnerable to a wide array of gelatinous and crustacean predators that dominate the upper mesopelagic zone. Despite this vulnerability, the energetic cost of producing such small offspring is low for the adult female, allowing her to allocate a greater proportion of her annual reproductive budget to a larger number of eggs per spawning event. The larval period is characterized by a critical transition to first exogenous feeding, which must occur before the yolk reserves are fully exhausted.

The maximum lifespan documented for Beardfish, under the ambient thermal regime of 13.4 °C [T = 13.4 °C] characteristic of its deep-water habitat, extends to approximately 14 years [am = approximately 14 years], or 5,110 days. This longevity places the species among the moderately long-lived members of the demersal fish community on the continental slope, a durability that is likely linked to its conservative metabolic strategy and the low predation pressure experienced at depth. Aging studies based on otolith microincrements have confirmed that growth slows markedly after the onset of sexual maturity, with the oldest individuals approaching the asymptotic total length of 29.4 centimeters very gradually. Senescence in this species is thought to involve a gradual decline in physiological condition rather than a dramatic post-spawning mortality event. The combination of slow growth, late maturity, and extended longevity aligns with the life-history characteristics of many other deep-sea fishes that experience stable, cold environments with limited seasonality in food supply. Such traits make the Beardfish particularly vulnerable to overexploitation should a directed fishery develop.
